name: lilypond
why: A text-based music engraving language where notation is code, a genuinely unusual way to write and typeset scores.

brief.what_it_is: LilyPond is a free music engraving program that turns a plain-text input file describing a piece of music into printed or on-screen sheet music. You write notes as letters and numbers, special commands with backslashes, and the program compiles the text into engraved output. The site says it covers classical, early, modern, vocal, tablature, lead sheet, educational, orchestral and even Schenker-graph work. The homepage lists 2.27.4 as the unstable release and 2.26.0 as the stable one.
brief.why_it_exists: The site says LilyPond is devoted to producing the highest-quality sheet music possible and to bringing the aesthetics of traditionally engraved music to computer printouts. It treats the text-input model as a deliberate choice, because a graphical editor would distract from engraving quality.
brief.how_it_works: The input file holds the notes of a piece, and LilyPond compiles it into a score. Music can be assigned to named variables so one source feeds both a transposed part and a concert-pitch full score, so changing a note updates both. Accidentals are placed automatically from note names such as -is for sharp and -es for flat, using Dutch note names by default with other languages available.
brief.install_notes: The brief's install path is Homebrew, which installs the executables lilypond, lilypond-book, convert-ly, abc2ly, etf2ly, lilymidi, lilypond-invoke-editor, midi2ly and musicxml2ly. I did not open the Download page, so I have no confirmed platform or first-run steps. The site points to separate Manuals and a Learning manual for beginners, and to third-party editing environments with syntax highlighting or a GUI.
brief.standout: Notation is code: you type a text file and the compiler does the engraving, rather than dragging notes on a toolbar. The site leans into that, with shared variables that keep score and parts in sync from one source file. It is also part of the GNU Project and free software under the GPL.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage news lists LilyPond 2.27.4 released October 20, 2026 and 2.26.0 released April 21, 2026, with download and manual links for both. I did not check a commit history.
brief.caveats: The site warns that new users often find text input odd and recommends reading the Learning manual before assuming something is broken. It has no graphical note entry itself; GUI editing comes from other projects. The homepage fetch had no install or platform detail. The text-input page's code examples did not come through as text, so I have no verbatim input samples.

entry.title: LilyPond
entry.tldr: A music engraving program where you type sheet music as plain text and a compiler typesets it into a score.
entry.deeper_look:
LilyPond takes a text file describing a piece of music, with notes written as letters and numbers and special commands marked by backslashes, and compiles it into engraved sheet music. The site says it covers classical, early, modern, vocal, tablature, lead sheet, educational and orchestral work, and even Schenker graphs.

The text-input model is a deliberate choice. In the project's words: "LilyPond is primarily concerned with producing top-quality engraved sheet music; creating a Graphical User Interface (GUI) would distract us from this goal." The aim is to bring the look of traditionally engraved music to computer printouts.

The idea underneath is that a score can be source code. Music can be assigned to named variables, so one source can feed both a transposed part and a concert-pitch full score, and changing a note updates both. Accidentals are placed automatically from note names: -is means sharp and -es means flat, with Dutch note names by default and other languages available. As the site puts it, "In some ways, LilyPond is more similar to a programming language than graphical score editing software."

Homebrew also installs converters for other formats: abc2ly, etf2ly, midi2ly and musicxml2ly bring existing music in, and convert-ly updates older input files to newer syntax.

entry.whats_unique: Notation is code. You write text and the compiler does the engraving, rather than dragging notes on a toolbar. Shared variables keep a full score and its parts in sync from one source file.
entry.caveats: The site warns that new users often find text input odd and recommends the Learning manual first; there is no graphical note entry, though third-party editors add it.
